title: The Danish-Israeli Association in Aarhus
body: The Danish-Israeli Association in Aarhus (DIF) works for friendship between Israel and Denmark and shares knowledge of Israeli society and Jewish culture. Founded 8 March 1976. Founded 8 March 1976 · Aarhus A friendship between Denmark & Israel . The Danish-Israeli Association (DIF) in Aarhus is one of several regional associations in Denmark, working for friendship between Israel and Denmark — and sharing knowledge of Israeli society, Jewish culture and the Hebrew language through lectures and events. title: About
body: The history, purpose and principles of the Danish-Israeli Association in Aarhus. A friendship association founded 8 March 1976. Home About History · Purpose · Activities About the Danish-Israeli Association. The Danish-Israeli Association (DIF) was founded in Aarhus on 8 March 1976 and is one of several regional associations in Denmark. We work for friendship between Israel and Denmark, and for nuanced understanding of Israeli society and Jewish culture. Who we are Most of DIF's members are “ordinary” people who have a personal interest in Israel — the land itself, the Jewish people, religion, the Hebrew language, music, Israeli literature, cuisine, art, history and other cultural issues. Some have travelled in Israel; others have lived in a kibbutz; others again are mixed Danish-Israeli married couples. DIF's members include Danes and Israelis alike — though the majority are Danes. For that reason we always encourage more Israelis to join us. Most members live in the region around Aarhus, where we hold our meetings. Aarhus is Denmark's second-largest city with around 300,000 inhabitants — and has, by the way, a friendship city in Israel: Petach Tikva . Our purpose DIF heightens knowledge among Danes about Israel and Jewish culture. We provide information about the situation in Israel, the Jews in Israel, and the overall conditions in the Middle East as we see it. We do not interfere with political affairs as such; our work is inspired by four principles. Four principles Cultural and human bonds. We seek to strengthen cultural relationships between Israel and Denmark, as well as everyday personal ties

title: Membership
body: How to join the Danish-Israeli Association in Aarhus. Membership fees, benefits and payment details. Home Membership Become a member You are welcome at DIF. Anyone — Jewish or non-Jewish — who adheres to the purpose and program of the Danish-Israeli Association can become a member, provided they are not a member of another organisation whose aims contradict ours. Per person 175 DKK /year A full year's membership — including magazines and member discount on the lecture series. Per couple 225 DKK /year For two people at the same address. Young 18–25 95 DKK /year Student rate for those who want to take part. What you receive as a member Access to the lecture series at member price (350 DKK) instead of 450 DKK. Invitations to extra lectures, wine tastings, concerts and other events — including those not advertised broadly. Bladet Israel three times a year (the Danish Zionist Federation and the friendship associations). Magbit-Nyt three times a year (Keren Hayesod / Den Danske Israelindsamling). Member newsletters and emails about upcoming activities. Voice and vote at the annual general meeting; the right to stand for the board. Eligibility for DIF's trips to Israel. How to join Bank transfer using the details to the right. Include name, address and email in the message. Email us with your name, address and contact details — we'll send the rest. Hand a slip with your details to a board member at one of our events. Pay the treasurer directly at one of our events. If you join at the same time as you sign up for the lecture series, you of course pay the member price for the series.

title: Culture
body: Israeli and Jewish culture — book and film reviews, Israeli literature, klezmer and Jewish humour including Dry Bones. Home Culture Books · Films · Music · Humour Israeli and Jewish culture. Reviews, notes and overviews of books, films, literature, music and humour — from Israeli contemporary art to classic Danish-Jewish voices. Books & authors Israeli literature A world literature in miniature. Israel houses several of the most important contemporary writers. A. B. Yehoshua Peace dove with burnt wings A. B. Yehoshua is one of Israel's greatest writers — perhaps alongside Amos Oz. In a striking statement he places the core of the Holocaust with Moses, who in his view "said we could be Jews and live everywhere at the same time". A frankness only possible from a Jewish artist in Israel. Amos Oz · translated by Hanne Friis A Tale of Love and Darkness Hanne Friis translated Oz's autobiographical masterpiece — 632 pages — from Hebrew into Danish. A vast, research-intensive task that captures Oz's childhood in 1940s Jerusalem, his mother and father, the birth of a family and a state. Etgar Keret The Bus Driver Who Wanted to Be God Existential desperation and grotesque humour go hand in hand in this collection of stories from modern Israel. Keret is entertaining, at times howlingly funny with his bizarre dark wit and his everyday, sometimes provocative language. Salt-of-the-earth Jewish humour at its finest. title: The history of the Danish Jews
body: 400 years of Danish-Jewish history — from Christian IV's invitation to the Sephardic Jews in 1622, through the rescue in 1943, to the Jewish community today. Home The history of the Danish Jews 400 years · 1622 → today The history of the Danish Jews. A summary spanning four centuries — from the first Sephardic Jew settling in Glückstadt under Christian IV, through changing rights and restrictions, the rescue of October 1943, and the living Jewish community in Denmark today. Before 1600 — absence In 1569 Frederik II issued an ordinance on foreigners in Denmark which contained articles on religion (at that time religious freedom did not exist in the country). The law effectively prevented immigration; foreigners could only obtain a lejdebrev (safe-conduct) by special royal permission. At that point there were probably no Jews in Denmark. When the first Jews actually arrived is not known with certainty. By European standards, Jews came relatively late to Denmark. The 1600s — the Sephardim arrive 1606 : The first Jew is mentioned in Copenhagen — though he had been baptised in Germany. 1619 : The first Jew, the Sephardi Dionis, arrives in Glückstadt, newly founded by Christian IV as a trading city. 1622 : Christian IV invites a group of Sephardic Jews to settle in Glückstadt. The king hopes that the wealthy and well-educated Sephardim might help revive a strained Danish economy. In 1628 the Jews of the city are granted free religious and trading rights. 1641 : Christian IV grants privileges to Jews already living in Hamburg, Altona and Wandsbek (then under the Danish crown). They are given freedom of religion, the right to a synagogue

title: October 1943
body: The story of the Nazi action against the Danish Jews in October 1943, and the rescue of 7,220 Jews to Sweden — one of the few bright moments of the war. Home Danish Jews October 1943 2 October 1943 — 9 April 1945 October 1943 — The rescue of the Danish Jews. On the night of 1–2 October 1943 the Nazi action against the Danish Jews was to be carried out. It did not go as planned. Within weeks, around 7,220 Jews and 686 non-Jewish spouses had crossed to Sweden — rescued by an ordinary population that decided to act. The secret warning On 28 September 1943 the German diplomat Georg Ferdinand Duckwitz leaked details of the planned action to Danish politicians. Within hours the warning had spread further — through the Jewish Community, resistance networks, doctors, priests and ordinary neighbours — to the Jewish population. When the Gestapo and the Danish police struck on the night of 1–2 October, most homes stood empty. Only 472 people were found and deported to Theresienstadt. The rest were already in hiding or on their way to the coast. The flight across the Øresund In the following weeks the Jews were channelled through an improvised network of doctors' offices, hospitals, churches and private homes down to the coasts of Zealand and Falster — and onward across the Øresund to Sweden in fishing boats, row boats and small craft. Many fishermen risked their lives. Some took payment; others did it for free. Sweden had opened its borders on 2 October 1943 and accepted everyone. title: Support humanitarian causes in Israel
body: Magen David Adom, Keren Hayesod, KKL and other humanitarian organisations you can support for the benefit of Israel's population. Home Support humanitarian causes Principle 4 · Humanitarian support Support humanitarian causes in Israel. One of DIF Aarhus's four guiding principles is to support humanitarian initiatives for the benefit of Israel's population. Below are some of the organisations whose work the association recommends — all independent of DIF, all with transparent accounts. Emergency aid · the Red Star of David Magen David Adom (MDA) Israel's Red Cross. The country-wide ambulance service, pre-hospital emergency care and blood bank. MDA runs thousands of volunteers and saves lives regardless of whether the patient is Jewish, Muslim, Christian, soldier, civilian or tourist. Recognised by the International Red Cross movement in 2006. mdais.org → Israel's development · since 1920 Keren Hayesod — United Israel Appeal Israel's primary fundraising organisation since 1920. Builds homes for new immigrants, funds youth movements, helps Holocaust survivors and supports peripheral communities. The Danish branch is known as Den Danske Israelindsamling (DDI) and publishes the magazine Magbit-Nyt , which DIF members receive. kerenhayesod.dk → Environment · since 1901 KKL — Keren Kayemeth LeIsrael Israel's oldest environmental organisation. Famous for having planted more than 240 million trees and developed the green areas of the desert. Manages water resources, parks and ecological restoration. title: Privacy policy
body: How the Danish-Israeli Association in Aarhus handles your personal data — GDPR compliance, consent and your rights. Home Privacy policy GDPR · Personal data Privacy policy How the Danish-Israeli Association (DIF) Aarhus handles your personal data. The association is the data controller and complies with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the Danish Data Protection Act. Data controller Dansk-Israelsk Forening (DIF), Aarhus CVR number: 40376445 Contact: dif_webmaster@yahoo.dk What information do we process? DIF Aarhus only processes information necessary to run the association's activities. This typically means: Member information: name, postal address, email address, phone number (if shared), year of joining. Membership payments: date and amount. The bank transaction itself is handled by the financial institution. Lecture series sign-ups: name and contact details. Contact enquiries: the content of emails you send us. We do not collect sensitive personal data (health, religious or political beliefs, ethnicity, sexuality, etc.). Legal basis and purpose Processing takes place to: fulfil the association's obligations to members (GDPR Art. 6(1)(b) — contract), send invitations and newsletters about the association's activities (consent, Art. 6(1)(a) — you can withdraw consent at any time), comply with legal requirements, e.g. the Danish Bookkeeping Act (legitimate interest / legal obligation, Art. 6(1)(c)).
